title: Where We Expect AMD EPYC 9006 CPUs in the era of Agentic AI
gist: Patrick Kennedy argues AMD's EPYC 9006 strategy has become much more expansive, splitting into a big SP7 socket (up to 256 cores, 600W, 1.6TB/s), a smaller SP8 socket (8-128 cores, 130-400W), a 1.1GB-L3 EPYC 9006X for HPC, and an LPDDR5X EPYC 9006 LP (Verano) AI host CPU aimed at NVIDIA Grace/Vera in Helios racks. The bifurcation mirrors Intel Xeon 6 and suits agentic AI load spreading beyond the AI Factory.

themes.theme: Defining the agentic-AI data center CPU

insights.claim: STH argues that defining a data center CPU in the agentic AI era is non-trivial because data centers contain many processors, from 500W triple-digit-core server CPUs to sub-6W Arm BMCs, rear-door heat exchanger controllers and power shelf controllers.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: CPU TAM estimates for agentic AI depend heavily on which processor population is counted.
insights.quote: we explored what it even means to be a data center CPU in the era of Agentic AI, because data centers run a lot of processors.

insights.claim: The ASPEED BMC in most servers is effectively its own computer, with its own firmware, memory, storage, network connectivity, web server and APIs inside the server.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: ASPEED holds a ubiquitous embedded processor socket in server infrastructure.
insights.quote: the ASPEED BMC in most servers runs its own firmware, has its own memory, storage, and network connectivity, runs its own web server and APIs

insights.claim: CPU vendors claim their chips are best for everything, but in practice that applies within certain swimlanes, and AMD's many EPYC 9006 variants reflect that segmentation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Investors should evaluate CPU competitiveness per workload segment, not on vendor-wide claims.
insights.quote: People who sell CPUs often say that their chips are the best for “everything”, but usually that “everything” is within certain swimlanes.

themes.theme: AMD expands its server CPU strategy

insights.claim: Kennedy believes AMD's server CPU strategy is becoming much more expansive with the EPYC 9006 generation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Broader SKU coverage lets AMD address more data center CPU segments and defend share against Intel and Arm.
insights.quote: I think AMD’s strategy on server CPUs is becoming much more expansive.

insights.claim: The AMD EPYC SP7 offers up to 256 cores and 512 threads in a 600W part, or up to 96 cores at up to 5GHz in a 500W part, with 1.6TB/s memory bandwidth that appears to be 16 channels of 12800MT/s MRDIMMs.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Rising per-socket power and bandwidth increase demand for high-end memory (MRDIMM) and power/cooling infrastructure.
insights.quote: Key stats are that you can get up to 256 cores and 512 threads (in a 600W part) or up to 96 cores and 192 threads at up to 5GHz (in a 500W part).
insights.locator: First, we have the AMD EPYC SP7

insights.claim: Of the nine public EPYC SP7 SKUs, five are 500W and two are 600W, with only one 64-core 300W part mentioned at the low end, showing how far server CPU TDPs have climbed.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: High-TDP CPUs push liquid cooling and higher rack power densities beyond GPU racks.
insights.quote: five of the nine public SKUs are 500W, and two more are 600W.
insights.locator: First, we have the AMD EPYC SP7

insights.claim: SP7 is no longer the sole flagship for AMD EPYC but one of several configurations that can be considered a flagship.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: AMD's lineup is diversifying away from a single halo product toward workload-specific flagships.
insights.quote: In previous generations, this was the flagship or “high-end” configuration. Now, it is one of many that can be considered a flagship.
insights.locator: First, we have the AMD EPYC SP7

insights.claim: The EPYC 9006 SP8 socket scales from 130W to 400W and from 8 to 128 cores, serving as the smaller-socket side of Venice.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: SP8 targets traditional racks where power limits make the SP7 impractical.
insights.quote: The other side of Venice is the SP8 socket version that scales from 130W to 400W and from 8 to 128 cores.

insights.claim: AMD's SP7/SP8 split mirrors Intel's Xeon 6700P and Xeon 6900P bifurcation into higher-end and lower-end sockets, which Intel planned years in advance, with AMD now following a similar approach using newer cores, memory and PCIe.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Validates Intel's platform segmentation choice while suggesting AMD now matches it with newer technology.
insights.quote: Intel’s product planning saw the need to bifurcate the market into a higher-end socket and a lower-end socket years in advance. AMD is now taking a similar approach.

insights.claim: Kennedy questions how Intel's 288-core Xeon 6900E fares when AMD offers a 256-core/512-thread part with much more memory bandwidth and I/O.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Suggests Intel's dense E-core part faces competitive pressure in high-density cloud sockets.
insights.quote: I am not sure how a 288-core Xeon 6900E series fares when there is an option in the market for a 256-core/512-thread version with much more memory bandwidth and I/O.

insights.claim: Agentic AI CPU load will fall partly in the AI Factory and substantially in other data centers, making a big socket for maximum performance plus a smaller socket for traditional racks the right strategy.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Agentic AI should drive general-purpose CPU demand outside GPU clusters, benefiting x86 server vendors broadly.
insights.quote: Part of the workload is in the AI Factory, but much of the load will also fall on other data centers.
insights.locator: I think this is a critical point

insights.claim: The AMD EPYC 9006X is an SP7 HPC-oriented CPU with 1.1GB of L3 cache (12MB per core), 1.6TB/s memory bandwidth and higher frequencies, succeeding the 2022 Milan-X and 2023 Genoa-X.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Continues AMD's 3D-cache server line, a differentiated product in HPC and cache-sensitive workloads.
insights.quote: With 1.1GB of L3 cache or 12MB L3 cache/ core, plus the 1.6TB/s of memory bandwidth and higher frequencies

insights.claim: Kennedy predicts the EPYC 9006X, arriving somewhat later than the rest of the line, should be a monster.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Later launch timing defers revenue but positions a strong high-margin SKU.
insights.quote: The interesting thing is that the EPYC 9006X will come out a bit later, but it should be a monster.

insights.claim: The industry is split between those who read Meta Muse's 2 vCPU environments as a reason to stuff maximum vCPUs per socket and those who favor sub-100 cores per socket maximizing memory bandwidth and per-core performance; the EPYC 9006X is the latter camp's ideal.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Which camp wins for agentic workloads determines whether dense-core or high-bandwidth CPUs capture agentic AI demand.
insights.quote: Others believe the right form is sub-100 cores per socket, maximizing memory bandwidth and per-core performance.

themes.theme: EPYC 9006 LP Verano vs NVIDIA Grace/Vera

insights.claim: The AMD EPYC 9006 LP brings LPDDR5X to the EPYC line and is, in STH's view, a direct competitor to NVIDIA Grace or Vera CPUs, designed to go into a Helios rack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: AMD is targeting the AI host CPU slot NVIDIA has captured with its own Arm CPUs in rack-scale systems.
insights.quote: To us, this feels like a direct competitor to an NVIDIA Grace or Vera CPU designed to go into a Helios Rack.

insights.claim: 8x GPU AMD Instinct servers over the past year have used 192-core Turin Dense, 64-core or 128-core Turin parts, but rack-scale designs appear to prioritize hitting a power envelope over maximizing cores per rack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Power budgets in rack-scale AI favor efficient host CPUs, shrinking the core-count content per GPU node.
insights.quote: It seems like the answer for these rack-scale designs is hitting a power envelope at the expense of having the most cores in the racks.
